The global games industry continues to be full of contradictions. It’s a landscape of incredible creative energy, where breakout hits made in months by solo devs can connect with players on the same scale as an enterprise launch. Yet many studios are still struggling to navigate a volatile market characterized by fierce competition, complex platform economics, discoverability challenges, and immense pressure to capture player attention.

A new, pragmatic approach to development is gaining traction – studios are reevaluating their priorities, prototyping faster and reducing development cycles to ship short, quality games to market as quickly as possible.

Operating a game studio today is a delicate balance of opposites. Leverage the increased productivity of AI tools behind the scenes, while being careful to avoid stigma from players, potential quality issues, and new workflow fatigue. Manage risk by producing smaller games, but make sure your games are unique enough to get noticed. Navigate the complex world of platforms and partnerships to maximize exposure, without losing sight of the player communities that define a game’s sustained success.

In last year’s gaming trends report, we explored how studios were strategically evolving to survive in this uncertain climate. This year in the 2026 Unity Game Development Report, we’re seeing the impacts of those changes begin to manifest. The central question has shifted from whether a studio can survive, to how it can build a resilient and sustainable future.

The analysis in this report draws on a comprehensive survey of 300 game developers – working across game engines, team sizes, and around the world – as well as unique, proprietary data from nearly five million developers¹ who engaged with the Unity Engine and ecosystem in 2025. In each trend, we’ve paired the charts and data with qualitative insights from real studios making games today. Together, these paint a picture of a community that’s adapting, innovating, and defining a new formula for success in a changing industry.

Studios see big opportunities in small games.

To manage risk and work more intentionally in an uncertain climate, studios are prioritizing smaller-scale, focused player experiences. This strategy has led to a noticeable increase in short, commensurately priced games selling millions of copies and generating significant revenue. Over half (52%) of developers surveyed say their teams are now focusing on smaller, more manageable projects this year, and this approach is supported by a shift towards diversifying revenue streams beyond core game sales.

About the data

The data in this report is drawn from the Unity Engine and portfolio of service products, including games made with Unity that send events through the platform. These solutions span mobile, PC, XR, web, social, and console gaming to provide a unique high-level overview of video game development trends.

Additional data for this report comes from a Cintᵀᴹ CATI (computer-assisted telephone interview) conducted between September 16 and October 3, 2025. The surveyed audience consisted of 300 game developers with a margin of error of +/-5.66% at a 95% confidence level. Developers were surveyed across four regions: AMER (Canada, U.S.); APAC (Japan, South Korea); EMEA (France, Germany, Spain, Turkey, U.K).; and SAMER (Brazil).

We take data privacy seriously and have omitted and/or anonymized information from this report that would individually identify any single game, developer, or publisher. Although we also include outside sources of information, the data shown in the charts and graphics is original to Unity.

We’d like to express our gratitude to every studio who contributed their time and insights.

Chapter 1

Studios see big opportunities in small games

Developers are prototyping more intentionally to make shorter games.

Studios are adapting to rapid technological and market shifts in games by focusing on agility and risk reduction in development, particularly during early iteration. This is influencing one of this year’s more noticeable trends: games from small teams achieving big success. From Schedule I² and PEAK³ to R.E.P.O⁴ and Megabonk⁵, 2025 saw an unprecedented number of tightly scoped, competitively-priced games – some made in just a few weeks – generating millions of dollars in revenue and attaining unprecedented levels of representation at awards shows⁶ From indie to enterprise, studios of all sizes are taking note, reducing their development cycles to produce more focused gaming experiences.

1.1 The majority of studios are shifting focus to smaller games.

How respondents say business strategies are impacting development

The majority (72%) of respondents indicate that game production is becoming more streamlined: More than half (52%) say they’re focusing on smaller, more manageable projects, and one in five (20%) say their development cycles are becoming more condensed. Established monetization strategies remain popular, however, with 26% of respondents saying their studios are doubling down on live service games with an increased emphasis on post-launch content and live ops.

BY THE NUMBERS

64% of respondents from studios with 10–49 employees say market conditions have led to a focus on smaller, more manageable projects.

PEAK | Landfall

1.2 Studios are funding development by diversifying their revenue streams.

How respondents say they’re setting themselves up for success

Studios are employing a broad variety of tactics to stay competitive. Looking at chart 1.2, studios are diversifying revenue streams beyond primary game sales (24%) through methods like merchandising, ad revenue, and work-for-hire services. Other popular approaches include maximizing live ops revenue (17%) and finding greater efficiencies through dev tools (13%). Responses also indicate that studios are making games with lower production costs (12%) and prioritizing rapid prototyping to reduce upfront investment risk (7%).

BY THE NUMBERS

36% of respondents from studios with 300+ employees say adding work-for-hire services has been a key strategy for weathering economic conditions.

Cult of the Lamb: Woolhaven | Massive Monster | Devolver Digital

1.3 For Unity developers, project development time has decreased dramatically.

Project hours per month dropped consistently year over year

Unity project development time has significantly decreased across the board. The median development time dropped 77% – from 91 hours in January 2022 to 21 hours by December 2025 – suggesting a faster baseline for the typical Unity project.

This trend isn’t limited to smaller projects; the 75th percentile (representing projects with the longest development timelines) also saw a massive reduction, falling from 344 hours to 127 hours over the same period. Even the largest Unity projects by player count (1M+ MAUs) are being made faster, with median development time dropping from a peak of 462 hours in March 2023 to a low of 86 hours in October 2025. This acceleration could be an indicator that, for Unity developers, game creation is becoming more efficient and consistent.

Outbound | Square Glade Games

1.4 URP adoption is on the rise.

Unity devs are favoring flexibility over fidelity

Fretless – The Wrath of Riffson | Ritual Studios

Unity Editor data shows that the Universal Render Pipeline (URP) saw a 13% increase in adoption over the past year: 42% of active projects with a build used URP in 2025, up from 29% in 2024. This is partly driven by an increase in projects created in Unity 6,⁷ the first version of the Engine to make URP the default render pipeline, but it correlates with the overall growth of lightweight, casual games.

This rise suggests Unity developers are increasingly prioritizing stylized visuals over ultra-realistic graphics. This approach may facilitate targeting a wider range of devices, which aligns with the broader business goals of diversifying revenue streams. Additionally, it suggests more Unity developers are making foundational decisions to keep the option for multiplatform porting open.

1.6 A significant majority of studios are making casual games.

Respondents on the themes represented in their catalog

Market pressure to reduce risk and deliver value quickly has led studios to focus on smaller, more manageable projects, which in turn influences the types of games they develop. With player backlogs growing⁸ due to the ever-increasing number of games launched each year – 2025 saw more video game releases than any year previously⁹ – shorter experiences can offer a more appealing time commitment.

While historically popular¹⁰ genres like role-playing games (55%), strategy (53%), and action/adventure (52%) remain the top choices among studios, this year’s thematic trend was more striking: Nearly three quarters (73%) of studios surveyed indicate that they develop casual games, a response that broadly aligns with a growing appetite among players for less time-intensive, low-friction experiences, often with co-op.¹¹

1.7 Studios are taking a leaner, more strategic approach to prototyping.

How respondents say prototyping has shifted at their studios in the past year

1.8 Most studios limit prototyping to three months or less.

How long respondents say they spend experimenting with gameplay

Small games are typically built around tight gameplay loops that encourage short, repeat sessions. To hone in on this compelling gameplay more quickly, studios are refining their approach to prototyping.

As we see in chart 1.8, a majority (67%) of developers surveyed indicate they’re keeping this phase of development brief: 46% spend between one and three months prototyping and 21% under a month. Nearly half (48%) of studios indicate they’ve become more selective about which prototypes to develop into full games over the last year. Others are finding efficiencies in the experimentation phase, shifting focus to rapid, low-fidelity prototyping (26%) and shortening prototyping cycles to reduce costs (17%).

Dreams of Another | Q-Games

Chapter 2

Studios are taking a prudent approach to AI tools.

Devs are investing in LLMs to help with back-end development and planning.

Over the past few years, many studios have been hesitant to discuss or adopt AI tools – particularly generative AI systems capable of producing front-end content – to avoid community criticism, mitigate potential quality issues, avoid adopting new workflows, and preserve the creative enjoyment of building games, among other reasons. However, since devs are looking for ways to improve agility and reduce risk, they recognize the potential time-saving and quality assurance benefits that AI tools can provide. Many surveyed respondents report using AI tools for more back-end development and planning tasks – parts of the workflow that involve repetitive work and benefit from streamlined outlining processes. This approach allows devs to dedicate more time to refining design and gameplay mechanics.

2.1 Devs are largely using AI tools for coding assistance.

How respondents describe their AI tool usage in gaming projects

Writing, debugging, and optimizing game code takes a long time, and it can make or break deadlines. In chart 2.1, 62% of polled devs list coding assistance as a reason for using AI tools.

When it comes to structuring a game’s story and integrating it with gameplay, developers need to make a series of decisions to create a meaningful experience for the player. While 44% of the surveyed respondents use AI tools for writing and narrative design, unsurprisingly, larger polled studios with over 300 team members lead the way with 53% adopting AI tools in these workflows.¹²

Ashline Racing: Born To Burn | Stratton Studios

2.2 AI tools are helping teams improve efficiency and enhance decision making.

How respondents benefit from AI tool usage

With studios striving to maximize their team’s output and speed up game development, AI tools are becoming a key player in their tech stack. In chart 2.2, 73% of polled respondents cite improving efficiency as the top advantage of AI use. Since solo devs and indie studios are looking to develop and deploy small games quickly, it’s understandable that 64% of studios surveyed with under 10 team members say they’re using this tech.¹³

Whether it’s design analysis, game testing, player behavior analysis, or more, 62% of surveyed respondents note improved decision making as the second most important benefit they see using AI tools. Breaking down the data further, studios of all sizes are saying they are making more informed decisions, averaging around 60% of respondents.¹⁴

BY THE NUMBERS

79% of polled devs with over 150 team members say that AI tools have helped them improve efficiency.

Chapter 3

Studios are seeking out more ways to reach the right players.

Devs are embracing large-reaching platforms and new markets to overcome discoverability issues.

As solo devs and indie studios continue to find success in the market and smaller games become more popular, the number of gaming projects has grown from 40,933,681 to 43,351,854 (+6%) over the past year.¹⁵ With the number of Unity developers rising by 1.2% year-over-year ¹⁶ and discoverability becoming increasingly challenging, studios are taking measured steps to invest further and broaden their reach to attract new audiences.

3.1 Competition is the biggest hurdle for mobile game developers today.

How respondents describe the largest obstacle in mobile gamedev

While it’s been said that competition breeds innovation, top quality, and high performance, devs are definitely feeling the pressure and financial strain. In chart 3.1, 33% of respondents cite competition as the biggest hurdle that mobile game developers currently face, while 30% list cost of user acquisition (UA). This comes as no surprise since UA costs are affected by the level of market saturation. In this case, it’s typically the studios with the deepest pockets that dominate.

It’s important to note that nearly one in five (17%) of the surveyed devs list discoverability as their biggest challenge.

BY THE NUMBERS

33% of respondents cite competition as the biggest hurdle that mobile game developers currently face, while 30% point to UA as their greatest challenge.

Pocket Champs: 3D Racing Games | MadBox Games

3.2 Game concept decisions are challenging game developers.

Game development obstacles for dev teams

When it comes to games across platforms, devs are trying to stand out and struggling to make decisions – in chart 3.2, 25% of polled studios say that collectively settling on an idea that is interesting and unique in the market is their biggest challenge.

Since discoverability is difficult and 19% of respondents cite growing and marketing their games as a hurdle, they cannot rely on the co-marketing they get from platform partners alone. They need to experiment, build a self-reliant strategy, and look for strong partners.

BY THE NUMBERS

28% of surveyed respondents with less than 10 team members say that collectively settling on an idea that is interesting and unique in the market is the biggest challenge in game development.

3.7 Studios have seen the most success in Southeast Asia.

Success in emerging markets

Although there are hurdles to entering a new market, they won’t stop studios from taking calculated risks to expand their playerbases. Chart 3.6 shows that 73% of devs surveyed identify India as the most desirable emerging market, with Malaysia trails in a distant second at 51%.

Unsurprisingly, in chart 3.7, our respondents say they have seen the most success in Central and Southern Asia and Southeast Asia, at 60% and 68% respectively.

Sonic Dream Team | SEGA HARDlight

Taken altogether, the data suggests that even though the developers are getting their games to market faster – making smaller games and not waiting for 100% perfection – they’re doing so strategically and with a comfortable level of risk.

The same can be said for their approach towards standing out against the competition and improving discoverability – they’re ensuring the concept is unique and interesting, making data-related decisions, and prioritizing digital platforms with the most potential for reach. At the same time, they’re being mindful of entering proven markets in a respectful and responsible way.

Chapter 4

Cross-play and competition are driving player engagement

Devs are focusing on the flexibility and availability of their games.

Since studios are struggling with discoverability, they are placing even more focus on player engagement strategies. To no one’s surprise, multiplayer games are still very popular. However, to stand out from the competition, many devs feel they need to take them further by making their games available across platforms, adding cross-play functionality, and increasing live ops usage and player engagement strategies. Dev also say they are doubling down on incorporating battles into their game concepts to increase playtime and engagement.

4.3 Studios are struggling with the pace of content and balance updates in multiplayer games.

Top multiplayer game development challenge for respondents

Even though multiplayer games are persistently popular, that doesn’t negate the fact that building them is notoriously difficult. In chart 4.3, 31% of our respondents say that their biggest obstacle while creating a multiplayer game is the pace of content and balance updates, with technological complexity coming in second with 23%.

Interestingly, a limited budget, while still present in the polled devs minds, came in the middle of the pack with 11%. In prior years, budget has always been foremost for devs when it came to multiplayer development, suggesting that economies of scale may be coming into play to make networked games less expensive to develop.

Chapter 5

The business of games is broadening in scope.

Developers are casting a wider net to capture new audiences and bring in new revenue streams.

In response to a shifting economic landscape and evolving player expectations, studios are increasingly expanding beyond traditional sales models. As we reported in our first trend, nearly a quarter of developers surveyed (24%) say they’re diversifying their revenue streams beyond core game sales. To maintain financial stability and foster long-term growth, these teams are employing a broad range of tactics: forming strategic partnerships both in and outside of games, exploring new game ideas in different genres, and broadening their presence by launching on new platforms and expanding into new markets.

5.1 More studios are taking creative risks, while others are relying on tried-and-tested methods.

How respondents say their studios strategize

Studios vary significantly in their approach to game development. Looking at the data in chart 5.1, the majority of developers surveyed (32%) say they’re developing new ideas in any game genre, indicating an appetite for innovation. Closely following this are studios taking a more market-driven approach, with 28% of respondents creating new games based on what’s trending and popular among players.

BY THE NUMBERS

42% of respondents from studios with 1–9 employees say they develop new ideas across a variety of game genres.

Roadside Research | Cybernetic Walrus

5.2 Studios are going all-in on cross-collaboration and partnerships.

Respondents on the strategies their teams are using to promote revenue growth

An overwhelming majority of respondents (82%) say they’re leveraging collaborations and partnerships within the games industry to promote revenue growth. In-game monetization remains a core revenue driver, with 57% of surveyed studios saying they are earning through in-app purchases like boosters, cosmetics, and currency, and 56% through paid DLC or subscriptions. Expanding audience reach is another core tactic, with more than half of studios indicating that they’re targeting additional platforms (52%), and 50% generating revenue through publisher sales.

Looking at chart 5.2, it may be surprising to see that only 14% of respondents say their studios are using webshops to promote revenue growth. In the fast-changing space of third-party payments, it seems likely more studios will start leveraging webshops to support the development of future titles as previously walled gardens begin to open up.

BY THE NUMBERS

74% of respondents from studios with 1–9 employees say they’re targeting additional platforms to promote revenue growth.

Fretless – The Wrath of Riffson | Ritual Studios

5.3 Desktop and mobile are the top platforms for expansion.

Where respondents plan to launch games next

When it comes to expanding the reach of their games, 30% of developers surveyed say they’re prioritizing desktop, with mobile close behind (28%). Handheld gaming platforms have emerged as a significant and growing secondary market: 16% of studios say they plan to target handhelds, edging slightly ahead of traditional consoles (13%).

BY THE NUMBERS

Studios with between 10 and 49 employees vary significantly based on their top choice for post-launch platform expansion: 24% say they prioritize desktop, 23% mobile, and 23% are focused on gaming handhelds.

Rain World: The Watcher | Videocult | Akupara Games

5.4 Developers see strategic diversification and improved player targeting as major opportunities.

How respondents think the games industry can grow

BY THE NUMBERS

30% of surveyed studios with less than 10 people say deeper integration and collaboration with non-gaming markets will help amp up gaming industry growth.

Looking at the industry as a whole, developers see strategic evolution as key to continued growth. 29% of respondents say that diversified business strategies will help the sector maintain momentum in a time when games are cementing their status as a mainstream pillar of entertainment and culture.¹⁸ 26% of developers surveyed see improvements in player targeting as an area of opportunity. 19% of respondents regard deeper integrations and partnerships with players outside of games as another source of untapped potential. This focus on cross-media collaboration underscores the blurring lines between games and wider entertainment.

Maximum Apocalypse | Mega Cat Studios

Conclusion

Last year’s report showed how studios shifted their strategies to deal with economic headwinds by adopting more risk-averse strategies – staying small and agile, broadening the types of multiplayer games they developed, relying on dependable platform strategies, expanding game worlds and content pipelines, and being more deliberate in how they used time-saving tools.

This year, the market’s volatility persisted, marked by intense competition, complex and ever-shifting platform economics, weak discoverability, and the ongoing struggle to hold player attention. Yet, there is also a strong current of potential and creativity running through the industry, fueled by breakout successes from solo and indie developers whose playerbases increasingly rival those of enterprise studios.

Studios continue to be mindful and deliberate as they shape their long-term strategies – using AI tools pragmatically, creating smaller games, adopting trusted awareness tactics, expanding into proven emerging markets, offering players more flexible and competitive experiences, and taking a balanced approach to diversifying their business models.

Big Farm: Homestead | New Moon Production

These five trends show how studios are tackling their work in 2025 – but effective strategies also have to be forward-looking. So what lies ahead?

Where things are headed

Predictions for the biggest trend in the next year

The chart above shows that developers expect indie studios to continue breaking out. 28% of devs surveyed believe enterprise studios will face growing competition from indies. Echoing the first trend in this year’s report, 17% think larger studios will respond by taking more creative risks on smaller games.

Respondents also expect live service games to remain strong, with 25% saying that established live titles will continue to dominate. Contrary to the fourth trend in this year’s report, 12% foresee an increase in noncompetitive multiplayer games over the next year. So where do devs think the industry’s heading in the longer term?

We spoke to five of the brightest minds in the business for insights into what the future might hold in store.

Cult of the Lamb: Woolhaven | Massive Monster | Devolver Digital

What’s in store for the next 5+ years?

What’s in store for the next 5+ years?

Anthony Tirone, Tech Tree Games

“Community involvement in the live ops process. Designing and implementing new features alongside community feedback has been a large pillar of our games and continues to become more important.”

Miguel Santirso, VOODOO

“More sophisticated live operations, more variety of gameplay and genres inside a single game, and deeper social mechanics. Games will continue turning into big platforms that retain players for very long.”

Eldar Huseinau , Playtika

“I think the biggest trend for developers in the near future will be AI. AI is already a spirit of the time and a defining force for game development.”

Maximilian Lubbers, Ritual Studios

“I think we will continue to see shorter development timelines, possibly paired with episodic releases for games. Having a game stuck in development for years can be very expensive, so economically it makes a lot of sense.”

Dan Rossati, SEGA HARDlight

“AAA games are costing too much to make so they will continue to struggle to innovate. I want to see a return to AA gaming where the experimentation typically found in Indie games can meet larger budget execution for the mainstream.”

Dev tips for the next 5+ years

Dev tips for the next 5+ years

Mike Oliva, MadBox Games

“My advice would be to have a clean code architecture in your project. We didn't take care of this before scaling multiple games, and it became difficult to maintain stability in the game for the long term.”

Alyssa Kollgaard, Akupara Games

“Build for signal, not scale; the hardest problem for devs is getting anyone to notice their game. Focus on scoping and shipping – getting something polished and small out the door beats something ambitious and unfinished any day!”

Uladzislau Dorashau, Playtika

“Stay curious, keep experimenting and enjoy the journey. If you embrace new ideas and use them wisely, even if you make some mistakes along the way, you will still move in the right direction, where the future of industry is being shaped.”

Tobias Schnackenberg, Square Glade Games

“Keep your scope small to reduce risk. In the current market, tightly focused, concise gameplay loops are essential. They allow teams to iterate quickly, deliver clear value to players, and maximize the impact of every design decision.”

Evan Losi, Tech Tree Games

“Focus on long-term growth. That means investing in quality of life improvements, support tools, and nice-to-haves as much as bringing on juniors to the team.”
